abstract: The Anthropic Economic Index report analyzes AI's economic impact through 5 million Claude conversations (1M Claude.ai and 1M API transcripts) from November 2025. The analysis introduces five new 'economic primitives'—foundational measures capturing task complexity, human/AI skills, use case, AI autonomy, and task success—to provide a comprehensive portrait of how Claude reshapes economic activity. Key findings reveal that 49% of jobs now use AI for at least 25% of tasks, augmentation has overtaken automation as the primary use pattern, and substantial geographic variation exists in adoption driven by GDP per capita globally and workforce composition within the US.
keyFindings: 49% of jobs use AI for at least 25% of their tasks (up from 36% in early 2025), with augmentation (52%) now exceeding automation (45%) as the primary use pattern on Claude.ai.

Claude usage remains highly concentrated in computer and mathematical tasks (34% of Claude.ai, 46% of API traffic), though concentration is decreasing on Claude.ai with educational instruction rising to 15% of usage.

Within the US, usage per capita among lower-adoption states is converging rapidly toward parity, with statistical estimates suggesting full equalization could occur within 2-5 years at a pace ~10x faster than historical technology diffusion.

Claude succeeds at tasks overall but with declining success rates on more complex tasks; factoring success rates into job exposure analysis roughly halves implied productivity gains from 1.8 to 1.0 percentage points annually.

Geographic variation in use cases reflects adoption stage: coursework use is highest in lower-income countries while work and personal use dominate higher-income countries, with education sophistication in user prompts nearly perfectly correlating with response sophistication (r > 0.92).
methodology: Analysis of 2 million anonymized Claude transcripts collected November 13-20, 2025: 1 million Claude.ai conversations (Free, Pro, Max users) and 1 million first-party API transcripts. Economic primitives were operationalized through privacy-preserving automated classification using Claude itself as a classifier on anonymized conversation data. Classifiers were validated against human researcher ratings on sampled transcripts (Claude.ai) and internal/synthetic data (API) for directional accuracy rather than exact precision. Geographic analysis uses IP geolocation data (excluding VPN/hosting services) mapped to ISO-3166 country and region codes. Diffusion rate estimates employ OLS, weighted least squares, and two-stage least squares regression modeling proportional convergence of state-level Anthropic AI Usage Index (AUI) toward steady state. Correlations calculated at country level (N=117 countries, minimum 200 observations) and US state level (N=50 states, minimum 100 observations).
qualifiers: Analysis based on three months of data; diffusion estimates from short-run changes carry high uncertainty and may not persist over longer periods. Privacy filters exclude cells with fewer than 15 conversations and 5 unique accounts (500 conversations and 250 accounts for request clusters), limiting analysis of low-usage geographies. Classifier performance is directionally accurate but may deviate from human ratings (e.g., education estimates may understate complexity for some tasks). API data restricted to single-turn interactions whereas Claude.ai includes multi-turn conversations, limiting direct comparability. Geographic analysis excludes Wyoming and Seychelles due to abusive traffic. Relationships between primitives are correlational, not causal—cannot determine if income or education drive adoption or serve as proxies for other factors. Productivity estimates reflect current model capabilities; reliability on longer-running tasks expected to improve. All analysis limited to Claude users; findings may not generalize to other AI systems.
